'''SeminaVerbi-press''' is the program that reads Catholic newspapers and magazines, and the blogs of their journalists, for SeminaVerbi. It introduces itself to the sites it visits with this user agent:

<code>SeminaVerbi-press/1.0 (+https://en.seminaverbi.bibleget.io/wiki/Semina_Verbi:Press_bot)</code>

== Who reads ==
The reader is the article pipeline of SeminaVerbi, part of the BibleGet project. It is operated by the '''Catholic Digital Commons Foundation''', a non-profit organization. It is not a search engine and it sells nothing.

== Why ==
SeminaVerbi writes about works of culture (films, series, books, music, art) and about artists, in the light of the Gospel. The Catholic press often discusses such works seriously. The bot looks for those articles so that our editors can:
* find works worth an article that SeminaVerbi does not have yet;
* cite the Catholic press, with a link to the article, in the articles that SeminaVerbi already has.

Every proposal for a new article is read and voted on by people before anything is written.

== How often ==
* Once a day; a run that was missed is made up for. The limits below are for the day (UTC), however many times the bot runs.
* At most 250 articles per day, across all the outlets it reads.
* One request at a time per site, at least 10 seconds apart, or more if the site's <code>robots.txt</code> asks for a longer <code>Crawl-delay</code>.
* On every run it reads a site's <code>robots.txt</code> before anything else there, and obeys it (RFC 9309). It reads feeds and sitemaps with conditional requests where it can, so an unchanged feed costs almost nothing; a sitemap index, and the archive of a blog while it is read for the first time, are fetched in full.
* If a site answers that it refuses the request (HTTP 401, 403 or 429), the bot stops reading that site for the day and does not try again by other means. A site that refuses it every day for a week is no longer read.

== What is kept ==
For each article: its link, title, date, outlet and language, and, for each work or person it discusses, at most three short quotations of no more than 25 words each, always shown with the outlet and the link to the article, and with its title and date when the article gives them. It also keeps which work or person it found (its Wikidata item), the scores and answers the assistant gives, how the article is credited, when it was found and last tried, and, for articles from ''L'Osservatore Romano'' and its journalists' blogs, a short numeric fingerprint (hashes only) used to recognise the same article on two sites. Of a site it keeps what conditional requests need, how far a blog's archive has been read, and the days the site refused it.

The full text of an article is never stored. It is read only while the bot works on it, and an automated assistant reads the title and opening of an article and the paragraphs around a mention, never more than about 150 words at a time, to judge whether the article is about a work of culture, treats it in the light of faith or values, and really discusses the work, and what it makes of it. When a proposal for a new article is prepared, the assistant reads the quotations kept again, with the other notes on the work. Those passages are sent to [https://typesafe.ai TypeSafe], the service that runs the assistant. The service's terms ([https://typesafe.ai/legal/mca customer agreement], [https://typesafe.ai/legal/privacy-policy privacy policy]) state that it does not train models on what it is sent.

== For how long ==
Nothing listed above is deleted yet, also for the articles that were read and not used; the one exception is the list of the articles read in a day, which is emptied on a later day. A link and its short quotations stay with the SeminaVerbi article or the proposal that cites them, like any other source.

== How to be left out ==
An outlet that does not want to be read can:
* write on the talk page of this page; or
* add a rule for <code>SeminaVerbi-press</code> to its <code>robots.txt</code>, for example:
<pre>
User-agent: SeminaVerbi-press
Disallow: /
</pre>
The bot obeys it from its next run.
